p.src: Entanglement Is Not Irreversibility

u.src: Entanglement Is Not Irreversibility
en: Entanglement Is Not Irreversibility

p.src: Begin with a distinction that is easy to lose in discussions of measurement. Suppose two spins arrive in a product state, interact, separate, and leave in an entangled state. Must the entanglement remain forever? No. The interaction was unitary, so another suitable interaction can undo it. One may reflect the spins, bring them together again, and arrange an inverse evolution that returns the pair to a product state. There is no law according to which entanglement itself only increases.

p.src: The situation changes operationally when one member of the pair is discarded. If an electron flies away into an uncontrolled environment, then the partner that remains nearby is still entangled with something, but the missing degrees of freedom are no longer available for the inverse operation. In principle the distant electron might be reflected back; in practice it is gone. This is the sense in which a measurement is irreversible for us: the correlations have spread into degrees of freedom that we do not control.

p.src: The State Available to Alice

u.src: The State Available to Alice
en: The State Available to Alice

p.src:
Let a composite system be divided into Alice’s degrees of freedom $a$ and Bob’s degrees of freedom $b$, with pure-state coefficients $\Psi(a,b)=\braket{a,b}{\Psi}.$ Alice does not have access to Bob’s laboratory. Her complete local description is therefore not generally a wave function. It is the reduced density matrix $\rho_A(a',a)
=
\sum_b \Psi^*(a',b)\Psi(a,b).$ The sum removes Bob’s label. What remains has one bra index and one ket index for Alice, and it contains every probability distribution that Alice can obtain by experiments performed entirely in her neighborhood.

p.src: Here Alice’s neighborhood and Bob’s neighborhood should be read broadly. Each may include apparatus, magnetic fields, technicians, and any other degrees of freedom with which that observer can interact. The claim of locality is not that Bob cannot change his own system. He may do so in many ways. The claim is that, while he remains distant, nothing he does locally changes Equation .

p.src: Bob’s Local Unitary

u.src: Bob’s Local Unitary
en: Bob’s Local Unitary

p.src:
First ignore Alice and describe Bob’s manipulation alone. If Bob changes a magnetic field or otherwise changes his local Hamiltonian, his wave-function coefficients undergo a unitary transformation, $\psi_M(b)
=
\sum_{b'}U_{bb'}\psi(b').$ In the composite language Alice’s index is a spectator: $\Psi_M(a,b)
=
\sum_{b'}U_{bb'}\Psi(a,b').$ Complex conjugation converts the ket transformation into the corresponding bra transformation, $\Psi_M^*(a',b)
=
\sum_{b''}\Psi^*(a',b'')U^\dagger_{b''b}.$

p.src:
Now recalculate Alice’s density matrix: $\begin{aligned}
\rho_{A,M}(a',a)
&=
\sum_b\Psi_M^*(a',b)\Psi_M(a,b) \notag\\
&=
\sum_{b,b',b''}
\Psi^*(a',b'')
U^\dagger_{b''b}U_{bb'}
\Psi(a,b') \notag\\
&=
\sum_{b',b''}
\Psi^*(a',b'')
(U^\dagger U)_{b''b'}
\Psi(a,b') \notag\\
&=
\sum_{b',b''}
\Psi^*(a',b'')\delta_{b''b'}\Psi(a,b') \notag\\
&=
\sum_{b'}\Psi^*(a',b')\Psi(a,b') \notag\\
&=
\rho_A(a',a).
\end{aligned}$

p.src: Why unitarity matters

u.src: Why unitarity matters
en: Why unitarity matters

p.src: Unitarity was not decorative. It supplied the identity in Equation . In earlier language, unitarity expresses the conservation of distinctions: two distinguishable state vectors remain distinguishable under reversible evolution. If Bob possessed even a slightly nonunitary deterministic evolution, $U^\dagger U$ would not be the identity. Alice’s reduced density matrix could then change immediately, giving Bob a means of signaling faster than light.

p.src: Collapse Changes Conditions, Not Distant Marginals

u.src: Collapse Changes Conditions, Not Distant Marginals
en: Collapse Changes Conditions, Not Distant Marginals

p.src: The beam-splitter example makes the uneasiness vivid. A single photon is placed in a superposition of two paths, one toward Alice and one toward Bob. If Alice’s detector clicks, the conditional state assigns zero amplitude to a later click on Bob’s path. It is tempting to say that Alice has instantaneously changed Bob’s photon.

p.src:
What Bob can observe without Alice’s record is different. Before receiving any message, he must average over Alice’s possible outcomes. That unconditioned average is described by his reduced density matrix, and it does not change. Alice’s click changes which conditional subensemble describes a run once her result is known; it does not change Bob’s local marginal distribution. The distinction between $\rho_B
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\rho_{B\mid A=\text{click}}$ is the distinction between no signaling and useful correlations.

p.src: The Einstein–Podolsky–Rosen discomfort nevertheless survives. A singlet can give us maximal knowledge of the whole while neither constituent has a pure local state. That reversal of the classical expectation—knowing the whole without assigning definite pure states to the parts—is not a signaling effect, but it is genuinely peculiar. To expose the peculiarity more sharply, turn quantum mechanics into a programming problem.

p.src: A Classical Simulator for One Spin

u.src: A Classical Simulator for One Spin
en: A Classical Simulator for One Spin

p.src:
Draw a spin apparatus on a computer screen. The user can orient it, press a measurement button $M$, and read $+1$ or $-1$. Inside the classical computer store two complex amplitudes, $\alpha_u,\qquad \alpha_d,
\qquad
|\alpha_u|^2+|\alpha_d|^2=1.$ Between measurements, the computer integrates the appropriate Schrödinger equation. A simulated magnetic field can make the amplitudes precess exactly as a real spin state would.

p.src: The one-spin simulator: an orientable apparatus and measurement button connected to a computer storing two amplitudes.

u.src: The one-spin simulator: an orientable apparatus and measurement button connected to a computer storing two amplitudes.
en: The one-spin simulator: an orientable apparatus and measurement button connected to a computer storing two amplitudes.

caption.en: The one-spin simulator: an orientable apparatus and measurement button connected to a computer storing two amplitudes.

p.src:
When the user presses $M$, a pseudorandom-number generator selects an outcome with Born probabilities $P(+1)=|\alpha_u|^2,
\qquad
P(-1)=|\alpha_d|^2.$ The computer displays the selected sign and then performs the state update. After $+1$, $(\alpha_u,\alpha_d)\longrightarrow(1,0),$ whereas after $-1$, $(\alpha_u,\alpha_d)\longrightarrow(0,1).$ It then resumes unitary evolution from the post-measurement state. If the user rotates the apparatus before pressing $M$, the computer changes basis and calculates the probabilities appropriate to the new axis.

p.src: Two Spins: Where Local Simulation Fails

u.src: Two Spins: Where Local Simulation Fails
en: Two Spins: Where Local Simulation Fails

p.src: Two spins in a product state remain easy. Give Alice one computer storing amplitudes $\alpha_u,\alpha_d$, and Bob another storing $\beta_u,\beta_d$. Each machine evolves and measures its own spin. No communication is needed because the joint coefficients factor: $\Psi(a,b)=\alpha_a\beta_b.$

p.src:
An arbitrary two-spin state requires four coefficients, $\alpha_{uu},\qquad
\alpha_{ud},\qquad
\alpha_{du},\qquad
\alpha_{dd},
\qquad
\sum_{a,b}|\alpha_{ab}|^2=1.$ A single central computer can store these numbers and evolve them with the four-dimensional Schrödinger equation. When either observer measures, the central machine samples the correct marginal probability, discards the incompatible components, renormalizes the surviving components, and continues from the conditional state.

p.src: What the hidden wires mean

u.src: What the hidden wires mean
en: What the hidden wires mean

p.src: A central random generator connected to both stations could coordinate the outputs. In an ordinary classical simulator those wires would also be communication channels. Bob could deliberately send a bit to Alice, and if the link were instantaneous the machine would violate locality.

p.src: The quantum system does not grant Bob that freedom. His allowed local transformations are unitary, and the reduced-density-matrix proof already showed that no such transformation changes Alice’s marginal statistics. The simulator’s wires are therefore a sign that ordinary classical bookkeeping has the wrong structure, not evidence that nature contains accessible superluminal cables.

p.src: The thought experiment also contains a premise that deserves daylight: the measurement settings are treated as independent choices. Alice and Bob decide when to press their buttons and how to orient their apparatuses without those choices being secretly fixed by the source variables. Once the observers and their decision mechanisms are included inside one closed physical system, the philosophical language of free choice becomes delicate. Operational Bell tests formulate the needed condition as measurement independence and arrange spacelike-separated, externally generated settings. The lecture leaves the metaphysics open while retaining the experimental premise.

p.src: From Spins to a Particle on a Line

u.src: From Spins to a Particle on a Line
en: From Spins to a Particle on a Line

p.src: Spins have carried the discussion from finite-dimensional vectors through entanglement and locality. Now enlarge the Hilbert space. Consider one particle moving on an infinite line. A position eigenstate is denoted $\ket{x},$ and means that the particle has definite position $x$. These kets form a continuously labeled basis. A general state is a superposition of them, and its position-space wave function is $\psi(x)=\braket{x}{\Psi}.$

p.src: Position is being used as a complete basis label. This does not say that a classical state can be specified by position alone, nor that the particle simultaneously has definite position and momentum. It says that every quantum state vector can be expanded in the position basis. Momentum will appear as an operator acting on those position-space coefficients.

p.src:
The Born rule now gives a probability density, $\rho(x)=|\psi(x)|^2.$ For a continuous variable, the probability of one exact point is ordinarily zero. The probability of finding the particle in an interval is $P(x_1<x<x_2)
=
\int_{x_1}^{x_2}|\psi(x)|^2\,dx,$ and normalization requires $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|\psi(x)|^2\,dx=1.$

u.src: Continuous Orthonormality and the Delta Function
en: Continuous Orthonormality and the Delta Function

p.src: For a discrete orthonormal basis, $\braket{a}{a'}=\delta_{aa'}.$ For a continuous basis the analogue is $\braket{x}{x'}=\delta(x-x'),$ where the Dirac delta vanishes for $x\neq x'$ and has unit area: $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta(x-x')\,dx'=1.$ One may picture it as a narrow spike of width $\epsilon$, height $1/\epsilon$, and fixed area, followed by the limit $\epsilon\to0$.

p.src: Functions are therefore vectors: they can be added, multiplied by complex scalars, normalized, and paired by an inner product. Physical wave functions on the infinite line are square-integrable, so functions that grow without bound at infinity are excluded. The generalized basis functions $\delta(x-x_0)$ sit just outside that Hilbert space but remain indispensable as distributional basis vectors.

p.src: Linear Operators on Wave Functions

u.src: Linear Operators on Wave Functions
en: Linear Operators on Wave Functions

p.src:
A linear operator maps one function to another while respecting superposition: $L(c_1\psi+c_2\phi)
=
c_1L\psi+c_2L\phi.$ An observable must be represented by a Hermitian operator. In the present notation the condition is $\braket{\phi}{L\psi}
=
\braket{L\phi}{\psi},$ or equivalently $\braket{\phi}{L\psi}
=
\braket{\psi}{L\phi}^*.$ For unbounded operators, this statement includes a domain and boundary conditions; the integrations below assume wave functions for which the boundary terms vanish.

p.src: Differentiation is anti-Hermitian

u.src: Differentiation is anti-Hermitian
en: Differentiation is anti-Hermitian

p.src:
Try the derivative $D=\frac{d}{dx}.$ It is linear, but integration by parts gives $\begin{aligned}
\braket{\phi}{D\psi}
&=
\int dx\,\phi^*(x)\frac{d\psi}{dx} \notag\\
&=
\left[\phi^*(x)\psi(x)\right]_{-\infty}^{\infty}
-
\int dx\,\frac{d\phi^*}{dx}\psi(x) \notag\\
&=
-\braket{D\phi}{\psi},
\end{aligned}$ where the boundary term vanishes. Thus $D^\dagger=-D.$ The derivative is anti-Hermitian rather than Hermitian.

p.src: Multiply by $-i$: $p=-i\frac{d}{dx}.$ Complex conjugation changes $-i$ to $+i$, while integration by parts contributes another minus sign. The signs cancel, so $p^\dagger=p$. Restoring units, $p=-i\hbar\frac{d}{dx}.$

p.src:
The expectation value makes its reality explicit: $\begin{aligned}
\expect{p}_\psi
&=
-i\int dx\,\psi^*(x)\frac{d\psi}{dx} \notag\\
&=
i\int dx\,\frac{d\psi^*}{dx}\psi(x) \notag\\
&=
\expect{p}_\psi^*.
\end{aligned}$ Any number equal to its own complex conjugate is real, as an observable’s expectation value must be.

p.src: The Canonical Commutator

u.src: The Canonical Commutator
en: The Canonical Commutator

p.src:
One more calculation reveals why the operator in Equation  deserves attention. In units with $\hbar=1$, act first with $x$ and then with $p$: $\begin{aligned}
(px\psi)(x)
&=
-i\frac{d}{dx}\bigl(x\psi(x)\bigr) \notag\\
&=
-i\psi(x)-ix\frac{d\psi}{dx}.
\end{aligned}$ Reverse the order: $(xp\psi)(x)
=
-ix\frac{d\psi}{dx}.$ Subtracting Equation  from Equation , $\bigl([x,p]\psi\bigr)(x)
=
\bigl(xp-px\bigr)\psi(x)
=
i\psi(x).$ Because this holds for every wave function in the operator domain, $=i,$ or, with units restored, $=i\hbar.$

p.src: The classical counterpart is $\{x,p\}_{\mathrm{PB}}=1.$ Dirac’s historical reasoning ran in the opposite direction from the present derivation. He began with the algebraic resemblance between antisymmetric Poisson brackets and commutators, postulated the correspondence $\longleftrightarrow i\hbar\{A,B\}_{\mathrm{PB}},$ and inferred that the momentum operator must satisfy the canonical commutator with position. Here we discovered $-i\,d/dx$ by repairing the derivative’s failure of Hermiticity and only afterward found the same algebra.

p.src: What Comes Next

u.src: What Comes Next
en: What Comes Next

p.src: The move from spins to particles has preserved the architecture while changing its scale. A continuously labeled basis replaces a finite list of basis vectors. Sums become integrals, Kronecker deltas become Dirac deltas, and column vectors become square-integrable functions. Position acts by multiplication, while momentum acts by differentiation.

p.src: The next tasks are physical rather than merely notational. Momentum probabilities require the momentum basis and Fourier transformation. Time evolution requires the Schrödinger equation for $\psi(x,t)$. Wave packets will then connect the abstract operator $p=-i\hbar\,d/dx$ to motion: their group velocity will be related to momentum divided by mass, and translation symmetry will explain momentum conservation. The commutator $[x,p]=i\hbar$ is therefore not an isolated trick. It is the hinge between the vector-space mechanics already developed and the quantum dynamics of particles.
